abstract: Super Hi-Vision, or ultrahigh-definition television (UHDTV2), has a 7680 × 4320 pixel video image and 22.2 multichannel sound. The 22.2 multichannel sound is ideally reproduced by three-dimensionally arranged loudspeakers. However, loudspeakers cannot be arranged in the ideal positions in some viewing environments. Therefore, a 12-loudspeaker system integrated with a flat-panel display has been developed. The system can reproduce three-dimensional sound without loudspeakers behind or at the side of the viewer. The front 11 channels, which surround the display or are positioned on the display, are played back by the stereophonic method. The other channels, which are set far from the display, are played back by binaural processing with the head-related transfer function (HRTF). Reproduction by convolution with the HRTFs, the sound propagation characteristics from the loudspeakers to each ear, makes it possible to reproduce the sound of channels played by loudspeakers behind or at the side of the viewer using only front loudspeakers.

authors.bio: Satoshi Oode received a B.S. degree in physics from Sophia University and a M.S. degree in computational intelligence and systems science from Tokyo Institute of Technology, Tokyo, Japan, in 1997 and 1999, respectively. He joined Japan Broadcasting Corp. (NHK) in 1999 and worked as video engineer in the Programs Engineering Center. Since 2001 he has been working at the Science & Technology Research Laboratories. His research interests include emotion evoked by music, psychoacoustics and three-dimensional acoustic space perception.
authors.name: Satoshi Oode

authors.bio: Kentaro Matsui joined NHK in 1998. He has been working at the NHK Science and Technology Research Laboratories since 2001. He is now engaged in the research of 22.2 multichannel sound system for Super Hi-Vision, a ultrahigh-definition TV, particularly the research of binaural rendering of 22.2 multichannel sound with a smaller number of loudspeakers for home use. His research interests include audio signal processing, the measurement and application of head-related transfer functions (HRTFs), and spatial audio reproduction.
authors.name: Kentaro Matsui

authors.bio: Satoshi Oishi received a B.S. degree in physics and an M.E. degree in applied physics from Waseda University, Tokyo, Japan, in 2003 and 2005, respectively. He joined NHK in 2005 and worked as a studio engineer in the Fukuoka broadcasting station. Since 2010 he has been working at the Science & Technology Research Laboratories and is engaged in the development of the audio signal processing.
authors.name: Satoshi Oishi

authors.bio: Takehiro Sugimoto received B.E. and M.E. degrees in electronic engineering from the University of Tokyo, Japan, in 1999 and 2001, respectively. He also received a Ph.D. in information processing from Tokyo Institute of Technology in 2013. He joined NHK in 2001 and worked as an audio engineer in the Programs Engineering Center. Since 2004 he has been working at the Science & Technology Research Laboratories. His research interests are the acoustic transducer, audio coding, and three-dimensional audio reproduction. He is currently engaged in MPEG standardization.
authors.name: Takehiro Sugimoto

authors.bio: Yasushige Nakayama received B.E. and M.E. degrees from Iwate University in 1992 and 1994, respectively. He then joined NHK and has worked in the Science & Technology Research Laboratories since 1996. Nakayama's research includes distance control of sound image, audio coding system, 3D virtual reality audio, 22.2 multichannel sound system for UHDTV, and audio transmitting for live performance.
authors.name: Yasushige Nakayama
